title: 第十二节论原因的或然性

content.value:
我在前面所说的关于偶然性的或然性，并不是为了其他的目的，而是为了协助我们解释原因的或然性，因为哲学家们普遍承
—265一

what the vulgar call chance is nothing but a secret and conceal’ d
cause. That species of probability, therefore, is what we must chiefly
examine.
The probabilities of causes are of several kinds; but are all de-
riv'd from the same origin，viz.the association of ideas to a present
impression. As the habit, which produces the association, arises from
the frequent conjunction of objects, it must arrive at its perfection by
degrees, and must acquire new force from each instance, that falls
under our observation. The first instance has little or no force : The
second makes some addition to it: The third becomes still more sensi-
ble; and' tis by these slow steps, that our judgment arrives at a full
assurance. But before it attains this pitch of perfection, it passes
thro′ several inferior degrees, and in all of them is only to be esteem’
d a presumption or probability. The gradation, therefore, from proba-
bilities to proofs is in many cases insensible; and the difference be-
twixt these kinds of evidence is more easily perceiv’ d in the remote
degrees , than in the near and contiguous.
'Tis worthy of remark on this occasion, that tho’the species of
probability here explain’ d be the first in order, and naturally takes
place before any entire proof can exist, yet no one, who is arriv′d at
the age of maturity, can any longer be acquainted with it. ′ Tis true,
nothing is more common than for people of the most advanc’ d knowl-
edge to have attain’ d only an imperfect experience of many particular
events; which naturally produces only an imperfect habit and transi-
tion : But then we must consider, that the mind, having form'd
another observation concerning the connexion of causes and
effects, gives new force to its reasoning from that observation; and
by means of it can build an argument on one single experiment,
when duly prepar′ d and examin’ d. What we have found once to
follow from any object, we conclude will for ever follow from it;
and if this maxim be not always built upon as certain, ' tis not for
want of a sufficient number of experiments, but because we frequently
一266一

认，普通人称为偶然性的东西仅仅是一种秘密和隐蔽的原因。因此，这种或然性就是我们必须主要加以考察的对象。
原因的或然性有几种，但都来自于同一根源，也即来自于观念与一个当下印象的联结。既然产生这种联结的习惯源自于各个对象的频繁的结合，那么它必定是达到了完满的程度，并且必然通过我们所观察的每一个例子而获得了一种新的力量。第一个例子有少许的或者干脆没有力量；第二个例子已经给它增添了一些力量；第三个例子变得更加明显；通过这些缓慢的步骤，我们的判断达到了充分的确信。但是，在它达到完美的程度以前，它经过了几个较低的程度，并且这些程度全都被看作是一种推测或者是一种或然性。因此，在许多情况下，从或然性到证明的进展程度是难以觉察的；这些各种证据之间的差异，在那些距离远的等级中要比在那些距离近的等级中更容易被感知到。
值得在这一场合中谈及的是：虽然在这里得以解释的这种或然性在次序上是第一，而且它自然地发生在任何完整的证明存在之前，但是没有一个达到成熟年龄的人还能熟悉这件事。的确，
对许多有高深知识的人们来说，没有什么比只是获取许多特殊事件的一种不完全的经验更为普通的了；这就自然地只是产生一种不完全的习惯和过渡。但是，我们必须进一步考虑下面的情形，
也即当心灵已经形成了关于因果联系的另外一种观察以后，它就给予它根据那种观察而进行的推理以一种新的力量，并且在经过适时的准备和考察的基础上依靠这种推理建立一个单一实验的论证。我们曾经发现随着任何对象而来的某种东西，我们断言这种东西将永远跟随这个对象；如果这个公理并不总是建立在确定的基础上，那并不是由于缺少了充足的实验，而是由于我
—267一

meet with instances to the contrary; which leads us to the second spe-
cies of probability, where there is a contrariety in our experience and
observation.
′Twou′d be very happy for men in the conduct of their lives and
actions, were the same objects always conjoin′ d together, and we
had nothing to fear but the mistakes of our own judgment, without
having any reason to apprehend the uncertainty of nature. But as’ tis
frequently found, that one observation is contrary to another, and that
causes and effects follow not in the same order, of which we have had
experience, we are oblig’ d to vary our reasoning on account of this
uncertainty, and take into consideration the contrariety of events. The
first question, that occurs on this head, is concerming the nature and
causes of the contrariety.
The vulgar, who take things according to their first appearance,
attribute the uncertainty of events to such an uncertainty in the cau
ses, as makes them often fail of their usual influence, tho’they meet
with no obstacle nor impediment in their operation. But philosophers
observing, that almost in every part of nature there is contain’ d a vast
variety of springs and principles, which are hid, by reason of their
minuteness or remoteness, find that’tis at least possible the contrarie-
ty of events may not proced from any contingency in the cause, but
from the secret operation of contrary causes. This possibility is conver-
ted into certainty by farther observation, when they remark, that upon
an exact scrutiny, a contrariety of effects always betrays a contrariety
of causes, and proceeds from their mutual hindrance and opposition.
A peasant can give no better reason for the stopping of any clock or
watch than to say, that commonly it does not go right : But an artisan
easily perceives, that the same force in the spring or pendulum has al-
ways the same influence on the wheels; but fails of its usual effect,
perhaps by reason of a grain of dust, which puts a stop to the whole
movement. From the observation of several parallel instances, phi-
—268—

们常常会遇到相反的例子；这就把我们引向了第二种或然性，在这种或然性中，我们的经验和观察含有相反的情况。
如果相同的一些对象总是彼此相连，并且除了我们在判断上的错误以外，再也没有任何事情可害怕，也没有任何理由忧虑那些本质不确定的东西，那么，人们在他们的生活和行动中将会感到十分幸福。但是，既然我们经常发现一个观察同另一个观察正好相反，并且那种原因和结果并不以我们已经经验过的相同的次序而出现，所以我们就被迫根据这种不确定而改变我们的推理，
并且考虑到各种结果的相反情况。发生在这个题目下的第一个问题就是关于这种相反情况的本质和原因。
普通大众根据最初的现象去考虑事物，他们将结果的不确定归结为存在着如此不确定的原因，以至使得事物虽然在其作用上未曾遇到任何障碍和阻挠，却常常不能发生着它们通常的影响。
但是，哲学家们注意到，自然中的每一部分几乎都包含有大量的动力和原理，由于这些动力和原理的微小或远隔，它们都被隐藏了起来。因此，他们发现，各种结果的相反情况至少“可能”不是来自于原因中的任何偶然性，而是来自于相反原因的秘密作用。
当他们在精确而又仔细的审查后注意到，结果的相反总是显露出原因的相反，并且总是产生于原因之间的互相妨碍和反对的时候，这种可能性就通过这种进一步的考察而变为确定的事情。为什么一架时钟或一只手表会停住不走，一个农民除了说它通常就走得不准以外，不能给出一个更好的理由。但是一个钟表匠却很容易察觉到，发条或钟摆的相同的力量对齿轮总是有相同的影响，它之所以不能产生通常的作用，其原因可能是一粒灰尘阻止了它的全部运动。通过对这几个类似的例子的观察，哲学家们形成了一269一

losophers form a maxim, that the connexion betwixt all causes and
effects is equally necessary, and that its seeming uncertainty in some
instances proceeds from the secret opposition of contrary causes.
But however philosophers and the vulgar may differ in their ex-
plication of the contrariety of events, their inferences from it are al-
ways of the same kind, and founded on the same principles. A contra-
riety of events in the past may give us a kind of hesitating belief for
the future after two several ways. First, By producing an imperfect
habit and transition from the present impression to the related idea.
When the conjunction of any two objects is frequent, without being
entirely constant, the mind is determin’ d to pass from one object to
the other; but not with so entire a habit, as when the union is unin-
terrupted, and all the instances we have ever met with are uniform
and of a piece. We find from common experience, in our actions as
well as reasonings, that a constant perseverance in any course of life
produces a strong inclination and tendency to continue for the future;
tho'there are habits of inferior degrees of force, proportion' d to the
inferior degrees of steadiness and uniformity in our conduct.
There is no doubt but this principle sometimes takes place, and
produces those inferences we draw from contrary phaenomena; tho′ I
am perswaded, that upon examination we shall not find it to be
the principle, that most commonly influences the mind in this
species of reasoning. When we follow only the habitual determi-
nation of the mind, we make the transition without any reflec-
tion, and interpose not a moments delay betwixt the view of one
object and the belief of that, which is often found to attend it. As
the custom depends not upon any deliberation, it operates imme-
diately, without allowing any time for reflection. But this method of
proceeding we have but few instances of in our probable reasonings;
270—

一个公理：所有原因和结果之间的联系都是同样必然的，而那种在一些例子中看起来是不确定的联系，都是产生于相反原因的秘密反对作用。
但是，不管哲学家们和普通人在说明结果的相反情况时意见是如何的不同，他们根据这种相反情况而进行的推论总是处于同一类型，并且是建立在同一原理之上。结果在过去的相反情况通过两种不同的方式可能会使我们对将来产生一种犹豫的信念。
第一种方式就是通过产生一个不完美的习惯和从当下的印象推导相关观念的不完美的过渡。当任意两个对象之间的联结是时常发生但并不是完全恒常不变的时候，心灵就被决定着由一个对象转移到另一个对象；但是决定心灵的那种习惯，却并不是一个完整的习惯，正如那种结合是不间断的，并且在我们曾经遇见的所有例子中都是整齐一致的那样。根据通常的经验，我们发现，
正如在我们的推理中一样，在我们的行动中，任何坚持不变的生命过程都会产生一种持续到将来的强烈的倾向和趋势；尽管对于在我们的行为中的较低程度的稳定性和一致性，也有与之相对称的较小力度的习惯。
毫无疑问，这个原理不时会发生，并且会产生我们根据相反现象得出的那些推论；不过我相信，一经考察，我们就会发现它并不是在这种推理中最通常影响心灵的那个原理。当我们仅仅是跟随心灵的习惯性决定时，我们就不经过任何反省而做出那种过渡，并且在看到一个对象和相信有通常发现伴随它的那个对象之间没有片刻的思想停顿。由于这种习惯并不依赖于任何审慎的考虑，所以它就立刻发生作用，不容许有任何反省的时间。但是，
我们在或然性推理中，只有这种行动方式的极少例子；它们甚至
271—

and even fewer than in those, which are deriv′ d from the uninterrupt-
ed conjunction of objects. In the former species of reasoning we com-
monly take knowingly into consideration the contrariety of past events;
we compare the different sides of the contrariety, and carefully weigh
the experiments, which we have on each side: Whence we may con-
clude , that our reasonings of this kind arise not directly from the hab-
it, but in an oblique manner; which we must now endeavour to ex
plain.
'Tis evident, that when an object is attended with contrary
effects, we judge of them only by our past experience, and always
consider those as possible, which we have observ' d to follow from it.
And as past experience regulates our judgment concerming the possi-
bility of these effects, so it does that concerning their probability; and
that effect, which has been the most common, we always esteem the
most likely. Here then are two things to be consider' d, viz. the rea-
sons which determine us to make the past a standard for the future,
and the manner how we extract a single judgment from a contrariety of
past events.
First wemay bserve,that the supposition,thatthefutrerese
bles the past, is not founded on arguments of any kind, but is deriv′ d
entirely from habit, by which we are determin′ d to expect for the fu-
ture the same train of objects, to which we have been accustom'′ d
This habit or determination to transfer the past to the future is full and
perfect; and consequently the first impulse of the imagination in this
species of reasoning is endow′ d with the same qualities.
But, secondly，when in considering past experiments we find
them of a contrary nature, this determination, tho′fulland perfect in
itself, presents us with no steady object, but offers us a number of
disagreeing images in a certain order and proportion. The first im-
pulse, therefore, is here broke into pieces, and diffuses itself over all
those images , of which each partakes an equal share of that force and
vivacity , that is deriv′d from the impulse. Any of these past events may
—272—

比由对象的不间断的结合而形成的那种推理中的例子更少。在前一种推理中，我们通常都会有意地考虑过去结果的相反情形；
我们将这种相反的情形的两个方面加以比较，并且仔细地衡量我们已经对每一个方面所做的实验，由此我们就可以得出结论：我们的这种推理不是直接地由习惯发生的，而是以一种间接的方式发生的；我们必须现在就要努力对这一点加以解释。
显然，当一个对象伴随有几个相反的结果时，我们仅仅是根据我们过去的经验对它们加以判断，并且总是认为我们已经看到的那些伴随这个对象而来的结果是可能的。由于过去的经验控制着我们关于这些结果可能性的判断，所以它也控制着我们关于这些结果的或然性判断；而我们总是认为那种最常见的结果是最为可能的。因此，有两件事情需要在这里加以考虑，也即：决定我们将过去作为将来的理由，以及我们从过去结果的相反情况中提取一个单一判断的方式。
首先，我们可以着到，那个“将来类似于过去”的假定并没有建立在任何一种论证的基础上，而完全是由习惯产生的，这种习惯，决定着我们去期待在将来也会有我们已经习惯了的相同系列的对象。这种由过去推移至将来的习惯或决定是充分和完美的；
因此，在这种推理中，想象的最初冲动被赋予了相同的性质。
其次，但是当我们考虑到过去的经验，发现它们的性质彼此相反的时候，尽管那种决定本身是充分和完美的，它呈现给我们却并不是稳定的对象，而是给予我们一些处于某种次序和比例中的不和谐的意象。因此，最初的冲动在这里就分裂成各个部分，
并且将自已散布在所有这些意象中，这些意象都分享了产生于那种冲动的同等的力度和活泼性。这些过去结果中的任何一个都
—273一

again happen; and we judge, that when they do happen, they will be
mix' d in the same proportion as in the past.
If our intention, therefore, be to consider the proportions of con-
trary events in a great number of instances, the images presented by
our past experience must remain in their first form, and preserve their
first proportions. Suppose, for instance, I have found by long obser-
vation, that of twenty ships, which go to sea, only nineteen return.
Suppose I see at present twenty ships that leave the port; I transfer my
past experience to the future, and represent to myself nineteen of
these ships as returning in safety, and one as perishing. Conceming
this there can be no difficulty. But as we frequently run over those
several ideas of past events, in order to form a judgment concerming
one single event, which appears uncertain; this consideration must
change the first form of our ideas, and draw together the divided ima-
ges presented by experience; since’ tis to it we refer the determination
of that particular event, upon which we reason. Many of these images
are suppos′ d to concur, and a superior number to concur on one
side. These agreeing images unite together, and render the idea more
strong and lively, not only than a mere fiction of the imagination, but
also than any idea, which is supported by a lesser number of experi-
ments. Each new experiment is as a new stroke of the pencil, which
bestows an additional vivacity on the colours, without either multipl-
ying or enlarging the figure. This operation of the mind has been so
fully explain’ d in treating of the probability of chance, that I need
not here endeavour to render it more intelligible. Every past experi-
ment may be consider' d as a kind of chance; it being uncertain to
us, whether the object will exist conformable to one experiment or an-
other : And for this reason every thing that has been said on the one
subject is applicable to both.
Thus upon the whole, contrary experiments produce an imperfect
belief, either by weakening the habit, or by dividing and afterwards
—274

可以再次发生；并且我们断定，当它们真正发生的时候，它们也会同过去一样，以同一的比例混合起来。
因此，如果我们的目的是要去考虑多数例子中的相反结果的比例，那么，由我们过去的经验所呈现的那些意象必然会保留在它们的最初形式中，并且保存有它们最初的比例。例如，假定通过长期的观察，我发现有二十艘船出海，只有十九艘返回。假定我现在看见有二十艘船驶出码头，于是我就将过去的经验转移到将来，并且声称这些船中只有十九艘将安全返回，一艘将沉没。
关于这一点并无任何困难。但是由于我们常常会匆匆浏览那些过去经验的各个观念，以便形成一个关于似乎并不确定的单个的结果的判断，所以这种考虑必定会改变我们观念的最初形式，并且将经验所呈现的分散的意象聚集起来；因为正是根据经验我们才谈及到我们所据以推理的那个特殊结果的决定。这些意象有许多被假定为同时发生，而且更多的意象就会合于一个方面。这些一致的意象彼此结合，并且使得那个观念不仅比一个仅仅是想象的虚构更强烈和生动，而且比为少数实验所支持的任何观念都更强烈和生动。每一个新的实验就好比铅笔新画的一笔，这一笔没有增加或者扩大那个图形，而是给颜色增添了一种活泼性。心灵的这种作用在论及偶然性的或然性时已经如此充分地解释过，
以至我在这里无需努力去更为清楚地提出它。每一个过去的实验都可以看作是一种偶然性，那个对象的存在将符合于其中的一个实验，还是符合于另外一个实验，对我们来说并不能确定；由于这一原因，我们关于上一个论题所说的一切也就适用于现在的论题。
因此，就整个来说，相反的实验或者通过减弱这种习惯，或者
—275—

joining in different parts, that perfect habit, which makes us conclude
in general, that instances, of which we have no experience, must
necessarily resemble those of which we have.
To justify still farther this account of the second species of proba-
bility, where we reason with knowledge and reflection from a contrari-
ety of past experiments, I shall propose the following considerations,
without fearing to give offence by that air of subtilty, which attends
them. Just reasoning ought still, perhaps, to retain its force, however
subtile; in the same manner as matter preserves its solidity in the air,
and fire , and animal spirits, as well as in the grosser and more sensi
ble forms.
First, We may observe, that there is no probability so great as
not to allow of a contrary possibility; because otherwise′ twou’ d cease
to be a probability, and wou' d become a certainty. That probability of
causes, which is most extensive, and which we at present examine,
depends on a contrariety of experiments; and’ tis evident an experi-
ment in the past proves at least a possibility for the future.
Secondly , The component parts of this possibility and probability
are of the same nature , and differ in number only , but not in kind. It
has been observ′ d, that all single chances are entirely equal, and
that the only circumstance; which can give any event, that is contin-
gent , a superiority over another, is a superior number of chances. In
like manner, as the uncertainty of causes is discover′ d by experi-
ence, which presents us with a view of contrary events,'tis plain,
that when we transfer the past to the future, the known to the un-
known, every past experiment has the same weight, and that′tis only
a superior number of them, which can throw the ballance on any
side. The possibility, therefore, which enters into every reasoning of
this kind, is compos′ d of parts, which are of the same nature both a
mong themselves, and with those, that compose the opposite probabil-
ity.

通过将那种完美的习惯分割为不同的部分，并在随后又将这些部分结合起来而产生一个不完美的信念。完美的习惯就是使我们大体地说，我们没有经验过的那些例子必然类似于我们已经经验过的那些例子的那种习惯。
在第二种或然性中，我们是由知识以及过去经验的相反情形而进行推理的，为了进一步地证明这种解释是正当的，我打算做如下的考虑，而不害怕由于这些考虑伴随有微妙的色彩而为人所责备。不管正确的推理是如何的微妙，它都仍然应该保持它的力量；正如物质不仅在更重、更能被感知的形式中，而且同样在空气、火和元气中都能保存它的充实性一样。
第一，我们可以说，没有任何或然性是如此的巨大以至不容许有任何相反的可能性；因为另外的情形将不再是一种或然性，
而是变成一种确定性了。我们目前正在考察的那种最为广泛的原因的或然性依赖于实验的相反情形，而且显而易见，过去的一个实验在将来至少会被证明是一种可能性。
第二，这种可能性和或然性的组成部分有相同的本质，而且它们仅仅有数量上的不同，而没有种类上的差别。前面已经说过，所有单一的偶然性都是完全相等的，并且能使任何一个可能发生的结果优越于另一个可能发生的结果的唯一条件就是一个更多数目的偶然性。在类似的方式中，既然原因的不确定被以呈现相反结果为目的的实验所发现，所以显而易见，当我们从过去推至将来，从所知推至未知的时候，每一个过去的实验都同等重要，并且仅仅多数的实验才能打破每一面的平衡。因此，每一个这种推理中所包含的可能性都是由相互之间本质相同、并且与组成相反可能性的那些部分的本质也相同的各个部分组成的。

Thirdly , We may establish it as a certain maxim, that in all mor-
al as well as natural phaenomena, wherever any cause consists of a
number of parts, and the effect encreases or diminishes, according to
the variation of that number, the effect, properly speaking, is a com-
pounded one, and arises from the union of the several effects, that
proceed from each part of the cause. Thus because the gravity of a
body encreases or diminishes by the encrease or diminution of its
parts, we conclude that each part contains this quality and contributes
to the gravity of the whole. The absence or presence of a part of the
cause is attended with that of a proportionable part of the effect. This
connexion or constant conjunction sufficiently, proves the one part to

因和结果而进行的推理都是建立在两个条件上，也即任何两个对象在所有过去经验中的恒常的结合，以及一个当下的对象与那两个对象中的任何一个的类似关系。这两个条件的作用就是，这个当下的对象激发并活跃了想象；这种类似关系连同恒常的结合，
将这种力量和活泼性传送到相关的观念中，因此我们就说相信或同意了这个对象。如果你减弱了这一结合或类似性，你就减弱了这种转移原理，结果也就减弱了产生于这种原理的那种信念。如果两个对象之间的结合并不是恒常的，或者如果当下的印象与我们常见的结合在一起的那些对象中的任何一个并不完全类似，最初印象的活泼性就不能完全传送到相关的观念中。在前述的那些偶然性和原因的或然性中，被减少的乃是结合的恒常性；而由类比所产生的或然性，受到影响的仅仅是类似关系。没有某种程度的结合和类似关系，就不可能有任何推理。不过既然这种类似关系容许有许多不同的程度，那么这个推理也就依其比例而有或多或少的稳固和确定的程度。当一个实验转移到与之并不精确的类似例子上的时候，它就失去了力量；不过显而易见，只要它保留有任何类似关系，这个实验就仍然可以保留作为或然性的基础的那种力量。
